blocks.text: A child with tonsillitis develops a tender, enlarged neck node. Under the microscope, the node shows large pale germinal centres in its outer zone because the node is where lymph-borne antigen meets lymphocytes, and where a response can be mounted locally.

blocks.markdown: Lymphoid organs are organised microenvironments controlling where antigen is trapped, where lymphocytes enter, where they proliferate and where they mature. The **lymph node** filters **lymph**, the **spleen** filters **blood**, and the **thymus** is the **primary** lymphoid organ in which T cells mature. Lymph nodes and spleen are **secondary** lymphoid organs where mature lymphocytes meet antigen.

blocks.title: Core terms
blocks.text: A lymphoid follicle is a rounded aggregate of mostly B cells; a secondary follicle has a pale germinal centre where B cells proliferate after antigen. A high endothelial venule (HEV) is a post-capillary venule with plump cuboidal endothelium through which blood-borne lymphocytes enter a node. Spleen white pulp is lymphoid tissue around central arterioles; red pulp is the blood-filled region of splenic cords and sinusoids. The thymus is a lobulated organ with a dense cortex and paler medulla.

blocks.title: Identifying node zones
blocks.prompt: A section shows an outer dense region with rounded follicles, a deeper follicle-free region rich in lymphocytes with cuboidal-lined venules, and a central region of pale channels between cords. Name the zones.

steps.text: Rounded follicles in an outer dense region are the cortex.
The deeper follicle-free zone with high endothelial venules is the paracortex, the T-cell zone.
Pale channels between cords of plasma cells and macrophages are the medulla, with medullary sinuses leading to the hilum.

blocks.markdown: **Spleen.** There is no cortex-medulla pattern, and no afferent lymphatics: blood arrives by the splenic artery and its branches, which run in trabeculae and then become **central arterioles**. **White pulp** consists of a **periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS)** of T cells around each central arteriole, with B-cell **follicles** attached, and a **marginal zone** at the edge where blood is first sampled for antigen. **Red pulp** consists of **splenic cords** (of Billroth) and **venous sinusoids** with discontinuous endothelium. Macrophages in the cords remove aged or abnormal erythrocytes that cannot squeeze through the slits in the sinus wall; red pulp also stores some platelets.

**Thymus.** The thymus is lobulated. In the **cortex**, immature thymocytes (double-positive for CD4 and CD8) are packed densely, making the cortex dark; here cortical epithelial cells present self-MHC molecules and thymocytes that recognise them are rescued (**positive selection**). Thymocytes that bind self-antigen too strongly are removed in the **medulla**, where medullary epithelial cells display a wide range of self-antigens (a process involving the AIRE protein) and drive **negative selection**, producing self-tolerance. The medulla is paler and contains **Hassall (thymic) corpuscles**, whorls of epithelial cells. A **blood-thymus barrier** protects developing cortical cells from circulating antigen. There are no follicles, and the thymus involutes with age, replaced by fat.

blocks.title: Spleen versus thymus on slides
blocks.prompt: One slide shows blood-filled sinusoids and macrophages with lymphoid islands around small arteries; another shows lobules with a dark outer zone, a paler inner zone and whorled epithelial bodies. Identify them.

steps.text: Blood-filled sinusoids and cords are red pulp; islands around small (central) arteries are white pulp, so the first organ is the spleen.
A dark outer cortex, pale medulla and whorled Hassall corpuscles identify the thymus.
The thymus lacks follicles; the spleen lacks a cortex-medulla pattern.

blocks.answer: Spleen (red and white pulp); thymus (cortex, medulla, Hassall corpuscles).

items: Node: cortex (B follicles), paracortex (T cells, HEVs), medulla (cords and sinuses).
Spleen: white pulp (PALS, follicles, marginal zone) and red pulp (cords, sinusoids, macrophage filtering).
Thymus: cortex (immature, positive selection), medulla (negative selection, Hassall corpuscles).

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Do not call spleen white pulp a cortex, and do not call the thymus a lymphoid follicle organ: the thymus has none. A node medulla holds cords and sinuses, whereas a thymic medulla holds Hassall corpuscles.

points: A node has cortex (B-cell follicles), paracortex (T cells and HEVs) and medulla (cords and sinuses), with lymph flowing from afferent vessels to the hilum.
Spleen white pulp (PALS, follicles, marginal zone) mounts immune responses; red pulp (cords and sinusoids) filters blood and removes aged erythrocytes.
The thymus matures T cells: positive selection in the cortex, negative selection and tolerance in the medulla.

questions.stem: A node from a patient with a viral infection shows expansion of the diffuse zone between the follicles and the medulla, with many cuboidal-lined venules. Which region has expanded and which cells fill it?

options.text: Paracortex, filled mainly with T cells
Cortex, filled mainly with plasma cells
Medulla, filled mainly with B-cell follicles
Subcapsular sinus, filled mainly with erythrocytes

questions.correctOptionText: Paracortex, filled mainly with T cells

distractorRationale.b: The cortex holds follicles with B cells.
distractorRationale.c: The medulla holds cords and sinuses.
distractorRationale.d: Lymph, not erythrocytes, flows through the subcapsular sinus.

questions.explanation: Follicle-free tissue between cortex and medulla with high endothelial venules is the paracortex, the T-cell zone. T-cell responses expand it during viral infection.

questions.stem: In a splenic section, a small artery lies in the centre of a sleeve of densely packed small lymphocytes. What is the sleeve?

options.text: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheath of the white pulp, rich in T cells
Splenic cord of the red pulp
Hassall corpuscle of the thymus
Medullary cord of a lymph node

questions.correctOptionText: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheath of the white pulp, rich in T cells

distractorRationale.b: Cords are macrophage-rich red pulp tissue.
distractorRationale.d: Medullary cords lie in lymph nodes.

questions.explanation: The central arteriole surrounded by lymphocytes is the hallmark of white pulp, and the surrounding sheath (PALS) is T-cell rich. B-cell follicles are attached to it.

questions.stem: A newborn has no thymic tissue and very few circulating T cells, though B cells are present. What explains the T-cell deficit?

options.text: The thymus is the site where T cells mature and are selected
The thymus is where B cells are filtered from lymph
The thymus is the main site of erythrocyte destruction
The thymus supplies lymph to the paracortex

questions.correctOptionText: The thymus is the site where T cells mature and are selected

distractorRationale.b: B cells do not mature in the thymus.
distractorRationale.c: Aged erythrocytes are removed in the spleen.
distractorRationale.d: Lymph reaches nodes by afferent lymphatics.

questions.explanation: Thymocytes arrive from marrow and mature in the thymus. Without the organ, T-cell maturation fails, so T-cell numbers are low while B cells are preserved.

questions.stem: After a patient's spleen is removed, a blood film shows abnormal or aged erythrocytes that would normally have been cleared. Which splenic structures normally perform this clearance?

options.text: Macrophages of the splenic cords in the red pulp
Germinal centres of white pulp follicles
Hassall corpuscles
High endothelial venules

questions.correctOptionText: Macrophages of the splenic cords in the red pulp
questions.explanation: Red pulp macrophages in the cords remove aged or abnormal erythrocytes that cannot pass through the sinus slits. White pulp has a different, immunological role.

questions.stem: Describe the cortex, paracortex and medulla of a lymph node, giving a key cell type or structure for each.
markingGuide: Cortex: outer, contains follicles and mainly B cells (germinal centres in secondary follicles).
Paracortex: deeper, T-cell zone with high endothelial venules for lymphocyte entry.
Medulla: central, medullary cords with plasma cells and macrophages, and medullary sinuses.
Efferent lymph leaves at the hilum.
questions.explanation: A complete answer gives position plus a recognisable cell or structure for each region.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces lymph through a node?

options.text: Afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, cortical sinus, medullary sinus, efferent lymphatic at the hilum
Efferent lymphatic, medullary sinus, cortical sinus, subcapsular sinus, afferent lymphatic
Afferent lymphatic at the hilum, medullary sinus, subcapsular sinus, efferent lymphatic
High endothelial venule, paracortex, medulla, hilum

questions.correctOptionText: Afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, cortical sinus, medullary sinus, efferent lymphatic at the hilum

distractorRationale.c: Afferent vessels enter through the capsule, not the hilum.

questions.explanation: Lymph enters through the capsule, percolates through successive sinuses and leaves at the hilum, which maximises contact with macrophages and lymphocytes.

questions.stem: Explain how the structure of the thymus supports positive and negative selection and the development of self-tolerance.
markingGuide: Immature thymocytes enter and proliferate in the dense cortex.
Cortical epithelial cells present self-MHC; thymocytes with useful recognition are rescued (positive selection).
In the medulla, epithelial cells (AIRE) and dendritic cells display self-antigens; strongly self-reactive thymocytes are removed (negative selection).
Mature, self-tolerant T cells leave the medulla.
Blood-thymus barrier in cortex or Hassall corpuscles mentioned as features.
questions.explanation: Structure matches function: cortex for expansion and positive selection, medulla for tolerance. The result is a T-cell repertoire that is both functional and self-tolerant.

questions.stem: A section of lymphoid organ has a dark outer zone packed with small lymphocytes, a paler inner zone with whorled eosinophilic bodies, and no follicles. Which organ is this?

options.text: Thymus
Lymph node
Spleen
Palatine tonsil

distractorRationale.c: The spleen has red and white pulp.
distractorRationale.d: Tonsils have follicles with germinal centres.

questions.explanation: A dark cortex, a paler medulla with Hassall corpuscles and absence of follicles identify the thymus. The other organs all contain follicles.

questions.stem: Rigid or abnormally shaped erythrocytes are retained in the spleen while normal ones pass. Which feature of the red pulp explains this?

options.text: Cells must squeeze through slits in the discontinuous walls of the venous sinusoids, past macrophages in the cords
Cells must cross a blood-thymus barrier of epithelial cells
Cells are filtered through the high endothelial venules of the paracortex
Cells must pass through germinal centres of white pulp

questions.correctOptionText: Cells must squeeze through slits in the discontinuous walls of the venous sinusoids, past macrophages in the cords

distractorRationale.b: That barrier is in the thymus.
distractorRationale.d: Germinal centres are not in the blood path of the red pulp.

questions.explanation: Blood from open-ended vessels flows through cords and must re-enter sinusoids through slits; stiff cells are trapped and phagocytosed by macrophages. This is why red pulp filters aged erythrocytes.

questions.stem: Distinguish the white pulp from the red pulp of the spleen by composition, location and function.
markingGuide: White pulp: lymphoid tissue around central arterioles with PALS (T cells), follicles (B cells) and marginal zone.
White pulp mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigen.
Red pulp: splenic cords and venous sinusoids filled with blood and macrophages.
Red pulp filters blood and removes aged or abnormal erythrocytes.
questions.explanation: White pulp is immunological and red pulp is a blood filter. The marginal zone lies between them.
